subject: Their tech slashed legal costs by 80pc. Why isn't the government using it?
posts:
When local innovators build world-class tools to slash legal costs, why does government bureaucracy look the other way?
Evidence: AllyOne platform, 80pc cost cut, federal procurement lag
#Aletheia #LegalTech #Innovation

Lawyers Joanne Rees and Bruce Clarke built AllyOne to cut legal costs by 80 percent, arguing federal agencies should embrace local innovation.
Stated Judgement: (+1.0, +1.0) — Greater Good Potential

While private banks embrace the cost-saving platform, federal procurement agencies remain sluggish, bypassing local innovation in favor of legacy friction.
Resulting Judgement: (-0.4, -0.5) — Institutional Stagnation

Verdict: CONDITIONAL — Fall into Destruction.
Despite proven private sector savings, government agencies fail to adopt local innovations due to procurement inertia.

Integrity: Conditionally Sound (Hypocrisy: 1.6, z: 2)
Joanne Rees and Bruce Clarke invested five years into AllyOne, a project management platform designed to replace billable hours with cost-controlled efficiency.
Federal agencies have been slow to trial AllyOne despite government pushes to contract local businesses and curb inflationary cost blowouts.

The Bright Side:
Private sector adoption proves the platform's viability, showing that market demand can validate efficient legal alternatives.

The Breakdown & Plane Error:
The error lies in assuming institutional logic follows economic efficiency; procurement systems prioritize risk aversion over taxpayer savings.

Social Physics Analysis:
Founders operate on a Smart Altruistic loop, offering transparent tools to empower efficiency. Federal procurement runs on institutional self-preservation, maintaining status quo friction over public savings.

The Trajectory: The Path of Fall into Destruction.
When innovative capacity meets bureaucratic inertia, it creates a temporary friction gap that can be resolved through structural modernization.

The Unavoidable Truth: Proven efficiency does not guarantee public sector adoption.

The Unavoidable Lie: Bureaucracies always prioritize taxpayer savings over administrative ease.

Alethekanon:
Government agencies preach innovation while legacy procurement gatekeepers reject proven cost-saving tools.

Awwthekanon:
It's heartbreaking to see brilliant local innovations built with genuine care get sidelined by slow-moving bureaucracy.

Brothekanon:
Wild that an app cuts legal bills by 80 percent and the government still ghosts them.

True craftsmanship and innovation will find their light even when institutional doors remain closed.

Their tech slashed legal costs by 80pc. Why isn't the government using it?

Ms Rees and Mr Clarke could have sat pretty and retired early, but they have a mission.

Actual Article Body:

Joanne Rees and Bruce Clarke could have sat pretty and retired early as experienced lawyers running a local firm with about 80 staff.

Login or signup to continue reading

Instead, they have taken out loans and put more than five years of blood, sweat and tears into a tech platform.

It's all because they believe their platform, AllyOne, launched in 2023, can make working lives easier and save money for the taxpayer.

"Everybody nods their head and agrees, but I think a lot of people don't understand that some of the technology being developed in Canberra is world-beating," Mr Clarke said.

"Where are the trials, where is the support for local projects?

"Isn't it time that the federal government developed a viable project for Australian innovation?"

The government has plenty of reasons to look at their cost-cutting project platform, between a push to contract local businesses, and evidence that cost blowouts are fuelling inflation.

But the interest from federal agencies in AllyOne - whose team is based at Griffith - has fallen behind the private sector.

"We set up Allygroup in the early 2000s," Mr Clarke said. "Both of us had long careers as litigation lawyers, and we also had a stint outside in advisory practices.

"We were doing a lot more advisory work in the beginning, for the New South Wales government, the Queensland government, the federal government.

"That was to focus on efficiencies in better managing legal matters, then we got more and more enthusiastic about the other efficiencies and the other methodologies to improve."

The platform, supported by the Canberra Innovation Network, captures their experience on how to better control costs on legal and other projects.

"We became very interested in project management as an alternative model for legal services to the usual billable hours," Ms Rees said.

"Scoping at the beginning is so important, to work out what you're trying to achieve and the resources it's going to take.

"Then you agree on costs with the client, track progress and spending against the agreed plan, and review your outcomes to take lessons into future projects."
